questions.text: 6 workers can build a wall in 10 days. How many days will 15 workers take to build the same wall, working at the same rate?
questions.explanation: Total work = 6 × 10 = 60 worker-days. With 15 workers, time = 60/15 = 4 days.

questions.text: Two cars start at the same time from cities P and Q, 360 km apart, and drive towards each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h respectively. How far from P will they meet?
questions.explanation: They close the gap at 120 km/h, so they meet after 3 hours. The car from P covers 50 × 3 = 150 km.

questions.text: A man rows downstream at 14 km/h and upstream at 8 km/h. What is the speed of the current?
questions.explanation: Speed of current = (downstream − upstream)/2 = (14 − 8)/2 = 3 km/h.

questions.text: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 504. If one of the numbers is 72, what is the other number?
questions.explanation: Product of the numbers = HCF × LCM, so the other number = 12 × 504 / 72 = 84.

questions.text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 15 hours. Pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. All three pipes are opened at 6:00 a.m. on the empty tank. At what time will the tank be full?
questions.explanation: Net rate = 1/12 + 1/15 − 1/20 = (5 + 4 − 3)/60 = 1/10 per hour, so it takes 10 hours: 6:00 a.m. + 10 hours = 4:00 p.m.

questions.text: Two trains 150 m and 210 m long are running on parallel tracks in the same direction at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. How long will the faster train take to pass the slower train completely?
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. Distance = 150 + 210 = 360 m. Time = 360/5 = 72 seconds.

questions.text: A container holds 50 litres of pure milk. 10 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This process is done once more. How much milk is now in the container?
questions.explanation: Each step keeps 4/5 of the milk. Milk left = 50 × (4/5)² = 32 litres.

questions.text: The five-digit number 7x86y (where x and y are single digits) is divisible by both 8 and 9. What is the value of x + y?
questions.explanation: For 8, the last three digits 86y must be divisible by 8, so y = 4 (864 = 8 × 108). For 9, the digit sum 7 + x + 8 + 6 + 4 = 25 + x must be a multiple of 9, so x = 2. x + y = 6.

questions.text: In a certain code, BOOK is written as 43. Using the same rule, how is PAGE written?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet and the values are added: B(2) + O(15) + O(15) + K(11) = 43. PAGE = 16 + 1 + 7 + 5 = 29.

questions.text: Find the odd one out: BDF, KMO, PRT, GIL
questions.explanation: In BDF, KMO and PRT each letter is 2 places after the previous one. In GIL, I to L is a gap of 3.
questions.topic: Logical reasoning: Odd one out (letter groups)

questions.text: Find the next number in the series: 1, 2, 6, 15, 31, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 1, 4, 9, 16, i.e. 1², 2², 3², 4². The next difference is 25, so 31 + 25 = 56.

questions.text: Starting at point P and facing north, Kabir walks 4 km. He turns 90° anticlockwise and walks 6 km, turns 90° anticlockwise again and walks 12 km, and then turns 90° clockwise and walks 2 km. Where is he now with respect to P?
questions.explanation: Positions: (0, 4) → west 6 → (−6, 4) → south 12 → (−6, −8) → west 2 → (−8, −8). He is 8 km west and 8 km south, i.e. 8√2 km to the south-west.

questions.text: P, Q, R, S and T each have a different number of books. Q has more books than only T. P has more books than R but fewer than S. Who has the third highest number of books?
questions.explanation: Q has more than only T, so T has the fewest and Q is fourth. Then S > P > R fill the top three, so the order is S, P, R, Q, T. R is third.

questions.text: 1 March 2028 falls on a Wednesday. On which day of the week did 1 March 2027 fall?
questions.explanation: Between 1 March 2027 and 1 March 2028 there are 366 days, because 29 February 2028 is included. 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days, so go back 2 days from Wednesday: Monday.

questions.text:
Each question below has two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements is sufficient to answer the question.

Question: How many students are there in Ankit's class?
I. Ankit's rank is 12th from the top and 15th from the bottom.
II. There are 8 more girls than boys in the class.
options: Both statements together are not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
questions.explanation: From I, the total is 12 + 15 − 1 = 26. II gives only a difference, not a total.

questions.text:
Statements:
All squares are circles.
No circles are triangles.

Conclusions:
I. Some triangles are squares is a possibility.
II. No squares are triangles.

Assuming the statements are true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, which conclusion(s) logically follow?
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: Every square is a circle and no circle is a triangle, so no square is a triangle (II follows). That makes 'some triangles are squares' impossible, so I does not follow even as a possibility.

questions.text:
The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error.

Each of the players / have been given / a new jersey / for the tournament.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'Each of the players has been given…'.

questions.text:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a coherent paragraph. Choose the correct order.

P. Within a few minutes, the sky grew dark and heavy drops began to fall.
Q. Rohit set out for the market on a bright afternoon without an umbrella.
R. By the time he reached the shop, he was completely drenched.
S. Halfway there, he noticed clouds gathering over the hills.
questions.explanation: Q introduces Rohit and the bright afternoon; S (halfway there) notes the clouds; P describes the rain that followed; R ends with him drenched at the shop.

questions.text:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Every monsoon, low-lying neighbourhoods in many cities flood within hours of heavy rain. Engineers point out that natural drains and lakes, which once absorbed excess water, have been filled in to make room for buildings. Restoring even some of these water bodies, they argue, would cost less than repeatedly repairing flood damage.

What is the main argument made by the engineers?
options: Cities should stop all new construction.
Flooding is caused mainly by poor weather forecasts.
Monsoon rainfall has increased sharply in recent years.
Restoring natural water bodies would cost less than repeatedly repairing flood damage.
questions.explanation: The engineers argue that restoring some lakes and drains would be cheaper than repeated flood repairs. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.text:
What does the phrase 'a fish out of water' mean in the sentence below?

Arjun felt like a fish out of water at the formal dinner.
questions.explanation: 'A fish out of water' describes someone who feels awkward in surroundings that are unfamiliar to them.

questions.text:
Choose the word or phrase closest in meaning to 'frugal' as used in the sentence.

The village is known for its frugal way of life.
questions.explanation: 'Frugal' means careful with money or resources, i.e. economical; 'wasteful' is its opposite.

questions.text:
Choose the correct indirect (reported) form:

The teacher said to us, "Do not use your phones during the test."
options: The teacher told us to not used our phones during the test.
The teacher said us not to use your phones during the test.
The teacher told us that do not use our phones during the test.
The teacher told us not to use our phones during the test.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported with 'told' + object + 'not to' + base verb, and 'your' changes to 'our'.

questions.text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.

I wish I ______ the answer to your question, but I do not.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' about a present situation that is not true takes the past tense: 'I wish I knew'.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences about an election is grammatically correct?
options: Who you think will win the election?
Who do you think will win the election?
Whom you think will win the election?
Whom do you think will win the election?
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the subject of 'will win' ('do you think' is inserted), so the subject form 'who' is correct, and the question needs 'do'.

questions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer c
Set c = 0
for (each i from 1 to 24)
    if ((i mod 4) == 0 OR (i mod 6) == 0)
        c = c + 1
    end if
end for
Print c
questions.explanation: Multiples of 4: 6 numbers; multiples of 6: 4 numbers; multiples of both (12, 24): 2. Count = 6 + 4 − 2 = 8.

questions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer a, b
Set a = 48, b = 18
while (a != b)
    if (a > b)
        a = a - b
    else
        b = b - a
    end if
end while
Print a
questions.explanation: Repeated subtraction (48, 18) → (30, 18) → (12, 18) → (12, 6) → (6, 6) ends at the GCD, 6.

questions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer c
Set c = 0
for (each i from 1 to 5)
    for (each j from 1 to 5)
        if (((i * j) mod 4) == 0)
            c = c + 1
        end if
    end for
end for
Print c
questions.explanation: Pairs where i × j is a multiple of 4: i = 4 or j = 4 gives 9 pairs, plus (2, 2). Total = 10.

questions.text: A square board is divided into a 4 × 4 grid of 16 equal small squares. How many squares of all sizes can be found on the board?

You have a 7-litre jug, a 4-litre jug and an unlimited supply of water. Each of these counts as one step: filling a jug completely, emptying a jug completely, or pouring from one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full. What is the minimum number of steps needed to have exactly 6 litres in one of the jugs?
questions.explanation: Fill the 7 L jug (7, 0); pour into the 4 L jug (3, 4); empty the 4 L jug (3, 0); pour the 3 L across (0, 3); fill the 7 L jug (7, 3); pour into the 4 L jug until it is full (6, 4). That is 6 steps, and a search of all jug states shows no shorter sequence exists.
